claims.text: An active-learning neural network potential trained iteratively on ab initio solid and liquid configurations near melting will be a more accurate reference potential than conventional EAM.
The active-learning neural network potential will be more transferable than conventional EAM.
The neural network potential will improve phase-space overlap with the target ab initio system.
The neural network potential will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by 30–50% relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
CoCrFeMnNi is a multicomponent high-entropy alloy relevant to the proposed study.
The relevant CoCrFeMnNi and related quinary systems include both solid and liquid states at or near their melting temperatures.
The proposed training set should iteratively incorporate diverse ab initio configurations from both solid and liquid states.
The intervention is applicable to near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys at temperatures within approximately ±10–20% of their melting point.
Solid and liquid high-entropy alloys in that temperature range exhibit a broad range of atomic configurations.
A neural network potential can flexibly represent the relevant potential-energy surface and many-body interactions.
Training on both phases allows the neural network potential to capture their configurational diversity.
Fixed-form EAM potentials are deficient at representing the full configurational diversity of high-temperature solids and liquids in these alloys.
Active learning from ab initio configurations corrects the stated EAM deficiencies.
Improved phase-space overlap produces a smoother and shorter thermodynamic-integration path.
Using the neural network reference will yield free-energy predictions closer to direct ab initio benchmarks.
TOR-TILD's conventional EAM references inadequately sample the variety of atomic configurations found in ab initio liquids.
Performance for extreme compositions or temperatures far below melting remains unverified.
Success depends on the representativeness and quality of the ab initio training data.
Failure to reduce path mismatch by at least approximately 30% relative to the EAM reference would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to improve agreement with a direct ab initio free-energy result would falsify the hypothesis.
